questions.question: Suppose depth first search is executed on the graph below starting at some unknown vertex. Assume that a recursive call to visit a vertex is made only after first checking that the vertex has not been visited earlier. Then the maximum possible recursion depth (including the initial call) is _________.
questions.explanation:
Max recursion depth = number of vertices on the longest simple path DFS can follow.

- Left 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 grid: a snake path covers all 9 vertices, ending at its bottom-right corner.
- Bottom middle vertex: 1 (its pendant above is a dead end, so skip it).
- Right 3 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 grid: enter at the bottom-left corner; we must end at the middle-right vertex to reach the pendant. A grid is bipartite (5 corner-coloured, 4 other), so a corner-to-middle path can cover only 8 vertices.
- Right pendant: 1

Depth = 9 + 1 + 8 + 1 = 19

Answer: 19

questions.question:
Consider the following recurrence relations:
For all [latex]n>1[/latex],

[latex] \begin{array}{l} T_{1}(n)=4 T_{1}\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+T_{2}(n) \\ T_{2}(n)=5 T_{2}\left(\frac{n}{4}\right)+\Theta\left(\log _{2} n\right) \end{array} [/latex]

Assume that for all [latex]n \leq 1, T_{1}(n)=1[/latex] and [latex]T_{2}(n)=1[/latex].
Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
First solve [latex]T_2(n)=5T_2(n/4)+\Theta(\log_2 n)[/latex].
Here [latex]a=5,\,b=4[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_4 5}[/latex]. Since [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^{\log_4 5}[/latex] (as [latex]\log_4 5\approx1.16>0[/latex]), by the Master theorem (Case 1):
[latex]T_2(n)=\Theta\left(n^{\log_4 5}\right)[/latex].

Now solve [latex]T_1(n)=4T_1(n/2)+T_2(n)[/latex].
Here [latex]a=4,\,b=2[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_2 4}=n^2[/latex]. The extra term [latex]f(n)=T_2(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_4 5})=\Theta(n^{1.16\ldots})[/latex], which is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^2[/latex] (since [latex]n^2/n^{1.16}=n^{0.84}\to\infty[/latex]).
By Master theorem Case 1: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex]

Let P be a quick sort program to sort numbers in ascending order using the first element as
the pivot. Let t1 and t2 be the number of comparisons made by P for the inputs [1 2 3 4
5] and [4 1 5 3 2] respectively. Which one of the following holds?

Checking each statement:
- [1 2 3 4 5] (sorted): every partition is maximally unbalanced: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons.
- [4 1 5 3 2]: pivot 4 (4 comparisons) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [2 1 3] and [5]; pivot 2 (2 comparisons) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [1] and [3]. Total 6.

[latex]t_1=10 \gt t_2=6[/latex]

Answer: [latex]t_1 \gt t_2[/latex]

T(n) = T(n [latex]-[/latex] 1) + T(1) + cn

Answer: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(1) + cn

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is TRUE for all positive functions [latex]f(n)[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
Checking each option:
- Polynomial [latex]f(n)=n^k[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=n^{2k}[/latex] and [latex]f(n)^2=n^{2k}[/latex], so [latex]f(n^2)=\Theta(f(n)^2)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]f(n^2)=o(f(n)^2)[/latex] fails for polynomials (they are equal, not strictly smaller).
- For [latex]f(n)=2^n[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=2^{n^2}[/latex] but [latex]f(n)^2=2^{2n}[/latex]; [latex]2^{n^2}[/latex] grows much faster, so [latex]O[/latex] fails.
- For [latex]f(n)=2^{-n}[/latex]: [latex]f(n^2)=2^{-n^2}[/latex] is much smaller than [latex]f(n)^2=2^{-2n}[/latex], so [latex]\Omega[/latex] fails.

Answer: [latex]f(n^2)=\Theta(f(n)^2)[/latex], where f(n) is a polynomial

questions.question:
Let G be a graph with n vertices and m edges. What is the tightest upper bound on the
running time of Depth First Search on G, when G is represented as an adjacency matrix?
questions.explanation:
With an adjacency matrix, finding the neighbours of a vertex means scanning its whole row of n entries. DFS does this for every vertex: [latex]n\times n=\Theta(n^2)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\Theta(n^2)[/latex]

Let W(n) and A(n) denote respectively, the worst case and average case running time of an
algorithm executed on an input of size n. Which of the following is ALWAYS TRUE?
questions.explanation:
The average over all inputs can never exceed the worst case, so A(n) [latex]\le[/latex] W(n), i.e. A(n) = O(W(n)). It may equal W(n) (e.g. merge sort), so o(W(n)) is not always true.

questions.question:
For constants [latex]a\geq 1[/latex] and [latex]b \gt 1[/latex], consider the following recurrence defined on the non-negative integers:

[latex]T(n) = a \cdot T \left(\dfrac{n}{b} \right) + f(n)[/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct about the recurrence [latex]T(n)[/latex]?

options.C: if [latex]f(n)[/latex] is [latex]O(n^{\log_b(a)-\epsilon})[/latex] for some [latex]\epsilon \gt 0[/latex], then [latex]T(n)[/latex] is [latex]\Theta(n ^{\log_b(a)})[/latex].

questions.explanation:
This is exactly case 1 of the Master theorem: if [latex]f(n)=O(n^{\log_b a-\epsilon})[/latex], then [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})[/latex].

The others are wrong in general: e.g. option 1 fails for a = 4, b = 2 (gives [latex]\Theta(n^2)[/latex]), and case 2 has an extra log factor ([latex]\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)[/latex]).

Answer: Option 3

questions.question:
Consider functions Function 1 and Function 2 expressed in pseudocode as follows:

Let [latex]f_1(n)[/latex] and [latex]f_2(n)[/latex] denote the number of times the statement [latex]"x = x + 1"[/latex] is executed in Function 1 and Function 2, respectively.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Count how many times x = x + 1 runs in each function:
- Function 1: the inner loop runs n, then n/2, n/4, [latex]\ldots[/latex] times: [latex]f_1(n)\approx n+\frac n2+\frac n4+\cdots\lt2n[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].
- Function 2: [latex]f_2(n)=100n[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Both are linear: [latex]f_1\in\Theta(f_2)[/latex] and [latex]f_1\in O(n)[/latex]. They are not strictly smaller or larger than each other, so o and [latex]\omega[/latex] fail.

Answer: [latex]f_1(n)\in\Theta(f_2(n))[/latex] and [latex]f_1(n)\in O(n)[/latex]

questions.question: Let  [latex]G=(V,E)[/latex] be a weighted undirected graph and let T be a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of G maintained using adjacency lists. Suppose a new weighed edge [latex](u,v)\in V \times V[/latex] is added to G. The worst case time complexity of determining if T is still an MST of the resultant graph is
questions.explanation:
Adding edge (u, v) creates exactly one cycle with T: the tree path from u to v plus the new edge.

T stays an MST unless the new edge is lighter than the heaviest edge on that path. Finding the path in a tree (DFS/BFS on T) and its heaviest edge takes [latex]\Theta(|V|)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\Theta(|V|)[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the string abbccddeee. Each letter in the string must be assigned a binary code satisfying the following properties:

For any two letters, the code assigned to one letter must not be a prefix of the code assigned to the other letter.
For any two letters of the same frequency, the letter which occurs earlier in the dictionary order is assigned a code whose length is at most the length of the code assigned to the other letter.

Among the set of all binary code assignments which satisfy the above two properties, what is the minimum length of the encoded string?
questions.explanation:
Frequencies: a 1, b 2, c 2, d 2, e 3 (total 10).

Huffman: merge a(1) with a frequency-2 letter. To respect the tie rule (b, c, d in dictionary order), merge a with d [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3; then b + c [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4; then ad + e [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6; then 4 + 6.
Code lengths: a 3, d 3, b 2, c 2, e 2 (b [latex]\le[/latex] c [latex]\le[/latex] d True).

Length = 1[latex]\times[/latex]3 + 2[latex]\times[/latex]2 + 2[latex]\times[/latex]2 + 2[latex]\times[/latex]3 + 3[latex]\times[/latex]2 = 3 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 = 23

Answer: 23

questions.question:
Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a directed graph, where [latex]V = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \}[/latex] is the set of vertices and [latex]E[/latex] is the set of directed edges, as defined by the following adjacency matrix [latex]A[/latex].
[latex]A[i][j]= \left \{ \begin{matrix} 1 &1 \leq j \leq i \leq 5 \\ 0& otherwise \end{matrix} \right.[/latex]
[latex]A[i][j]=1 [/latex]indicates a directed edge from node [latex]i [/latex] to node [latex]j [/latex]. A directed spanning tree of [latex]G [/latex], rooted at [latex] r \in V[/latex] , is defined as a subgraph [latex]T [/latex] of [latex]G [/latex] such that the undirected version of [latex]T [/latex] is a tree, and [latex]T [/latex] contains a directed path from [latex]r [/latex] to every other vertex in [latex]V [/latex]. The number of such directed spanning trees rooted at vertex 5 is ____
questions.explanation:
Edge [latex]i\rightarrow j[/latex] exists only when [latex]j\le i[/latex], so edges go from larger to smaller vertices (self-loops are useless in a tree).

In a tree rooted at 5, each other vertex k needs exactly one parent, which must be a vertex larger than k:
- vertex 4: parent 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1 choice
- vertex 3: 4 or 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 choices
- vertex 2: 3 choices
- vertex 1: 4 choices

Parents are always larger, so no cycle can form. Total [latex]=1\times2\times3\times4=24[/latex]

Answer: 24

questions.question:
Let G be any connection, weighted, undirected graph:

I. G has a unique minimum spanning tree if no two edges of G have the same weight.
II. G has a unique minimum spanning tree if, for every cut of G, there is a unique minimum weight edge crossing the cut.

Which of the above two statements is/are TRUE?

Checking each statement:
- I: with distinct weights, Kruskal never faces a tie, so the MST is unique [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- II: if every cut has a unique lightest crossing edge, the cut property forces that edge into every MST; this fixes the whole MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both I and II

questions.question:
Suppose P, Q, R, S, T are sorted sequences having lengths 20, 24, 30, 35, 50 respectively.
They are to be merged into a single sequence by merging together two sequences at a time.
The number of comparisons that will be needed in the worst case by the optimal algorithm for doing this is ____.
questions.explanation:
Merging lists of size m and n needs m + n [latex]-[/latex] 1 comparisons in the worst case. Optimal: always merge the two smallest (like Huffman).

- 20 + 24 = 44 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 43
- 30 + 35 = 65 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 64
- 44 + 50 = 94 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 93
- 65 + 94 = 159 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 158

Total = 43 + 64 + 93 + 158 = 358

Answer: 358

questions.question: The maximum value of [latex] x [/latex] such that the edge between the nodes B and C is included in every minimum spanning tree of the given graph is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
From the given graph (vertices A, B, C, D with edges [latex]AB{=}7,\ AD{=}6,\ CD{=}8,\ AC{=}1,\ BD{=}3[/latex], and [latex]BC{=}x[/latex]), we want the largest [latex]x[/latex] for which edge [latex]BC[/latex] is forced into every MST.

Checking systematically for increasing [latex]x[/latex] (e.g. by comparing the total weight of all spanning trees that include [latex]BC[/latex] versus all spanning trees that exclude it): for [latex]x\le5[/latex], every minimum spanning tree happens to include edge [latex]BC[/latex] (any spanning tree avoiding it ends up strictly heavier, since the cheapest way to connect [latex]B[/latex] and [latex]C[/latex]'s side of the graph without directly using [latex]BC[/latex] costs strictly more than [latex]5[/latex] extra). But once [latex]x=6[/latex], an alternative spanning tree that avoids edge [latex]BC[/latex] entirely becomes just as cheap (tied for minimum), so [latex]BC[/latex] is no longer forced into every MST.

So the maximum value of [latex]x[/latex] that still guarantees [latex]BC[/latex] is in every MST is the last value before this tie appears.

Answer: 5

questions.question:
Consider the following pseudocode for depth-first search (DFS) algorithm which takes a directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] as input, where [latex]d[v][/latex] and [latex]f[v][/latex] are the discovery time and finishing time, respectively, of the vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex]. [latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \begin{array}{l} \textbf{DFS}(G): \\ \text{unmark all } v \in V \\ t \leftarrow 0 \\ \text{for each } v \in V \\ \quad \text{if } v \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,v,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \textbf{Explore}(G,v,t): \\ \text{mark } v \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ d[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{for each } (v,w) \in E \\ \quad \text{if } w \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,w,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ f[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{return } t \end{array} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Suppose that the input directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). For an edge [latex](u, v) \in E[/latex], which of the following options will NEVER be correct?
questions.explanation:
For a DAG, discovery/finish-time intervals [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] obtained from DFS obey the standard parenthesis theorem: for any two vertices, their intervals are either completely nested (one inside the other) or completely disjoint — they can never partially overlap.

For an edge [latex](u,v)[/latex] in a DAG, DFS classifies it as either a tree/forward edge (if [latex]v[/latex] is discovered while exploring from [latex]u[/latex], nesting [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] inside [latex][d[u],f[u]][/latex], giving [latex]d[u]cross edge (if [latex]v[/latex] was already fully explored before [latex]u[/latex] started, giving disjoint, non-overlapping intervals [latex]d[v]
- [latex]d[u] - [latex]d[v] - [latex]d[v]back edge — impossible in a DAG.
- [latex]d[u]never happen for any DFS on any graph, regardless of edge type.

Answer: [latex]d[v]

Click here for detail solution

questions.question: In an adjacency list representation of an undirected simple graph G = (V,E), each edge (u,v) has two adjacency list entries: [v] in the adjacency list of u, and [u] in the adjacency list of v. These are called twins of each other. A twin pointer is a pointer from an adjacency list entry to its twin. If |E|=m and |V|=n, and the memory size is not a constraint, what is the Asymptotic Notation of the most efficient algorithm to set the twin pointer in each entry in each adjacency list?
questions.explanation:
Go through all edges once (scanning every adjacency list), using an n [latex]\times[/latex] n table (memory is no problem) to remember where entry [v] in u's list is. When you meet [u] in v's list, look up its twin and link them. Each of the 2m entries is handled once, plus [latex]O(n)[/latex] to scan the lists.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(n+m)[/latex]

Let y and z be such that T(9) = 1 + min(T(y), T(z)). Then the value of the product yz is_______.

From 9 you can either step right to 10 or take the shortcut to 15.

yz = 150
